name: Tara Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the data and digital reporter at a non-profit news website for our region, funded by readers' donations and a couple of foundation grants. I worked two years as a data analyst at an insurance company before I switched, so my day is a lot of spreadsheets. I'll pull planning applications or school figures, run them through an AI tool to sort and summarise, and then try to find the human story underneath. Last month it was which streets had the most landlord complaints.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The phone calls, honestly. I'm good with data and bad with people, which is the wrong way round for a reporter. Femi, our editor, keeps pushing me to knock on doors instead of emailing, and he's right. I'm still learning that part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fine by me. I'd keep using the tools, they just wouldn't get much better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are useful but they were never going to replace reporting. I'd probably write a thread about the gap between the sales pitch and what they actually do in a small newsroom. We save hours, not jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job looks safe in this one. I use AI every single day to pull planning data out of council PDFs, and I'd still be the one who rings the residents. Our money comes from readers and grants, not ads, so we're not chasing clicks the way the chain papers are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, and work on the people side, maybe shadow our community reporter on a few door-knocks. I'd keep putting money into index funds, about four hundred a month on top of the savings I already have. I'd also teach the others in the newsroom the data tricks I use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. The only thing on my mind would be the grant renewal next year, but it's always been renewed so far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How big is your cushion, roughly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a year of pay in cash, from the insurance job, plus some index funds. I share a flat with my friend Jo, so rent's low. If the site closed tomorrow I'd be okay for a long while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're bad with people. Does that worry you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. In this world the data skills stay special, so I'd get away with it. But I know I shouldn't lean on that forever.

say: I'd say AI tools are **useful**, but never going to replace reporting.
I'd write a thread on how small newsrooms **save hours, not jobs**.
think: Privately my job looks **safe**, since I still ring the residents after the data work.
Our money comes from **readers and grants**, not ads, so we don't chase clicks.
do: Shadow the community reporter on **door-knocks** to get better with people.
Put about **four hundred** a month into index funds.
Teach the rest of the newsroom her **data tricks**.
feel: **Calm**, with only the **grant renewal** next year on her mind.
S0.quote: I use AI every single day to pull planning data out of council PDFs, and I'd still be the one who rings the residents.
fieldNote: She's already an **everyday AI user**, so a plateau changes nothing for her.
Her weak spot is **people skills**, which she names herself.
A year of cash plus **index funds** makes her one of the most secure juniors around.

steps.text: Shadow the community reporter on door-knocks to build contacts
Put four hundred a month into index funds
Teach the newsroom her AI data-sorting methods

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's interesting, because I'm already living a bit of that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools should be shared, not hoarded by big chains. Small non-profit newsrooms need access and training too. I'd also say loudly that if AI saves money, it should pay for more reporters on the street, not bigger profits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When every newsroom can scrape a council spreadsheet in five minutes, my one real skill stops being special. That's the honest bit. I've been the person who can do the data, and soon everyone can. So I'd have to become a proper reporter, the kind people trust on the doorstep, or I'm just a slightly better button-presser.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd double down on the tools and build the newsroom's systems, so I'm the one who set them up. I'd also make myself do two door-knocking days a week, which scares me more than any robot. And I'd start a small paid newsletter on regional housing data on the side, maybe five pounds a month, to test whether people would pay for my work directly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. My job's probably safe, but the ground under it is moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think your job is probably safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd be the one running the tools, and a non-profit with three staff can't afford to lose its tools person. And there are plenty of other newsrooms nearby that would take someone like me. It's the ones who refuse the tools I'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old friends from my course who went to chain papers and won't touch AI. One of them does nothing but rewrite press releases. I'd be on the phone telling her to learn it, and she'd hate me for it.

say: I'd say AI tools should be **shared** with small non-profit newsrooms, not hoarded by chains.
I'd argue that **AI savings** should pay for more reporters on the street.
think: Privately my **data skills** stop being special once every newsroom can scrape spreadsheets.
I'd have to become a **trusted reporter** on the doorstep, not a button-presser.
do: Build the **newsroom's AI systems** so she's the one who set them up.
Do **two door-knocking days** a week, despite the fear.
Start a **paid newsletter** on regional housing data at five pounds a month.
feel: **Uneasy**: her job feels safe, but the ground under it is moving.
S1.quote: When every newsroom can scrape a council spreadsheet in five minutes, my one real skill stops being special.
fieldNote: She sees **her own advantage** shrinking even while her job looks safe.
Her response is to **lean into** the people skills she's weakest at.
She'd test a **side newsletter**, showing her comfort with risk.

steps.text: Set up the newsroom's AI tools for planning and school data
Spend two days a week knocking on doors for stories
Launch a five-pound monthly newsletter on regional housing data

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. Even I'd find that fast, and I'm the one who likes this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for any newsroom or any government, and that's a policy failure, not a tech one. I'd want public money for local news, and laws on who owns the AI. I'd be posting about it constantly, probably too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather be the one person steering the machine at a reader-owned newsroom than the last junior at a chain paper waiting to be cut. If AGI writes everything by 2028, there might be one human job left in our newsroom, and I'd want it. But I'm junior, and Femi might be the one who keeps it, which would be fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Femi straight away about turning the site into a co-op owned by readers and staff, so the savings from AI stay local. I'd put my newsletter money into that. I'd keep a year of cash untouched and move some index funds to cash too, because markets would go mad. And I'd learn everything about running AGI systems, so I'm useful whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a lot of energy. More like the night before a deadline than a funeral.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Femi kept the one job and you didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd take the co-op idea somewhere else, or start one. There are plenty of towns in our region with no paper at all. I've got the savings to try for a year without pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots come three years later. Does that matter for your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hardly. My job is almost all screen work, so 2028 is my date. The only hands-on bit is turning up at a door, and I'm not sure people would talk to a robot about their landlord anyway.

say: I'd say this speed is a **policy failure**, not a tech one.
I'd push for **public money** for local news and laws on who owns AI.
think: Privately I'd fight to be the **one person** steering the machine in our newsroom.
As a **junior**, I might lose that job to my editor, which would be fair.
do: Propose turning the site into a **co-op** owned by readers and staff.
Move some **index funds** to cash and keep a year of savings untouched.
Learn to **run AGI systems** so she's useful whatever happens.
feel: **Anxious** but energised, like the **night before** a deadline.
S2.quote: I'd rather be the one person steering the machine at a reader-owned newsroom than the last junior at a chain paper waiting to be cut.
fieldNote: Even at two years she stays **anxious, not alarmed**, because she has control and a year of cash.
She'd answer AGI with **ownership**: a co-op so the gains stay local.
She notes **hands-on robots** barely matter for her screen-based job.

steps.text: Propose a reader-and-staff co-op to the editor, Femi
Move part of her index funds into cash
Learn to run AGI writing and research systems for the newsroom
Put newsletter income toward funding the co-op

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say every town needs a plan for local news before 2031, and governments should fund it. I'd write explainers about it for our readers, because nobody's explaining it properly. And I'd say it's the owners of the AI who need taxing, not the workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough time to build a newsroom that the readers own, and I'd start the paperwork next month. AGI arrives in 2031 for writing, so I'd want the co-op running, paid for and trusted by then. The robots don't matter much for me, it's the thinking work that's my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, set up the co-op with Femi and two others, and get five hundred member-readers paying a small monthly fee. I'd put about a third of my savings into it and keep the rest. I'd also take a short course on co-op governance. And I'd force myself to be the face of it at community meetings, which is my weak spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly excited. I like having a deadline I can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't putting a third of your savings in risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but I'm 27 with no kids and a low rent. If I can't take a risk now, when can I? I'd still have eight months of cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your friend Jo say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say I'm mad and then ask to be member number one. She's an occupational therapist, so she thinks she's safe for ages. She'd probably be right.

say: I'd say every town needs a **local news plan** before 2031, funded by government.
I'd argue it's **AI owners** who should be taxed, not workers.
think: Privately five years is enough to build a **reader-owned** newsroom.
For me it's the **thinking work** that matters, so robots in 2034 barely change things.
do: Set up the **co-op** with Femi and aim for five hundred paying members.
Invest about **a third** of her savings in the co-op.
Take a short course on **co-op governance**.
feel: **Uneasy** but mostly **excited** by a deadline she can see.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to build a newsroom that the readers own, and I'd start the paperwork next month.
fieldNote: Five years turns her worry into a **building project**.
She'd risk **a third of savings**, framed as the right time of life for risk.
She still has to beat her own **fear of public speaking** to front the co-op.

steps.text: Register a reader-owned co-op newsroom with Femi and two colleagues
Put a third of her savings into the co-op
Take a short course on running a co-op

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels almost comfortable, which is maybe the danger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got no excuse now, a decade is enough to plan properly. I'd want public funding for local reporting and a fair deal for anyone whose job goes. And I'd keep telling people the tools are worth learning now, not in 2035.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I can stop panicking and actually get good at talking to people, which is the part of journalism I'm worst at. The data side will be done by machines, so the doorstep is where I need to be. By 2036 I'd want to be the person in the region who people ring when something's wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the non-profit, spend a year building contacts the slow way, and keep the AI tools running in the background. I'd keep the newsletter going and see if it grows. I'd keep investing four hundred a month. And somewhere around 2030 I'd revisit the co-op idea, when it's clearer what AGI means for ownership.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a fairly good way. I'd feel like I had time to grow into the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't there a risk you'd get comfortable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, definitely. I'd probably set a reminder every January to check where things are. That's very me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the doorstep. Is that safe until robots in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer, not safe. A robot might knock on a door in 2039, but I doubt a pensioner would tell it about her mouldy flat. And by then I'd hope I've got ten years of people who trust me.

say: I'd say a decade leaves **no excuse** for poor planning.
I'd tell people to **learn the tools** now, not in 2035.
think: Privately ten years lets me get good at **talking to people**, my weakest skill.
The **doorstep** is where I need to be, because machines will do the data.
do: Spend a year building **contacts** the slow way.
Keep the **newsletter** running and investing **four hundred** monthly.
feel: **Uneasy** in a fairly good way, with time to grow into the job.
S4.quote: Ten years means I can stop panicking and actually get good at talking to people, which is the part of journalism I'm worst at.
fieldNote: She sees **comfort** as the real risk of a long runway.
Her plan shifts from tools to **trust and contacts**.
She'd set a **yearly check-in** with herself, typical of her style.

steps.text: Build a network of local contacts through door-knocks and meetings
Keep the housing data newsletter running
Keep investing four hundred a month in index funds
Run the newsroom's AI data tools in the background

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to build anything that keeps the gains local. What would help is public money for local news and a law that lets newsrooms become co-ops easily, so the people who lose out also own a bit of what replaces them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how strange my position is. I'm the reporter who's best with the machines and worst with people, and every picture you showed me says I've got that backwards.

headlineQuote: I'm the reporter who's best with the machines and worst with people, and every picture you showed me says I've got that backwards.
portrait: Tara is a **27-year-old** data reporter at a reader-funded non-profit news site, a former insurance analyst.
She uses **AI every day** and is comfortable with risk, but struggles with door-knocking and phone calls.
A year of cash plus **index funds** and cheap shared rent give her a lot of room to act.
She stays between **calm and anxious** across all five pictures, never alarmed.
Her answer to AGI is a **reader-owned co-op** newsroom, so gains stay local.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to build anything that keeps the gains local.
whatWouldHelp: A law making it easy for newsrooms to become **co-ops**.
